A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MeshAnything and contain readable text, equations, figures and tables. The complete documents support comparison, including v2's appendix, which retains several analyses originally in v1's main text.

before.justification: v1 reports original mesh-generation examples, noise-resistant-decoder ablations and quantitative comparisons with Marching Cubes and remeshing in Figures 1–6 and Tables 1–3.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds human-preference studies, generation-benchmark results, conditioning comparisons and input-quality robustness experiments.

M1.justification: The point-cloud conditioning, transformer VQ-VAE, Gumbel-noise decoder fine-tuning and autoregressive generation procedure remain unchanged in Section 4. The expanded pipeline diagram and training description clarify existing components rather than introduce a different method.

E1.justification: Objaverse and ShapeNet coverage and the previously illustrated generation/reconstruction applications are retained. Appendix A.2 adds explicit test scenarios with Gaussian-corrupted point coordinates and normals. Naming Rodin for existing generation applications does not establish a newly covered task.

E2.justification: v1's external quantitative comparison contains Marching Cubes and remeshing variants. v2 additionally evaluates retrained PolyGen and MeshGPT in Tables 1–2, Shape As Points in Tables 1 and 5, and FlexiCubes in Table 5, including remeshed variants of the latter extraction methods. Figure 3 also introduces unconditional and image-conditioned controls.

E3.justification: v2 adds generation-baseline retraining, preference studies with 30 outputs per method and 41 participants, and COV, MMD, 1-NNA and wireframe-image FID/KID evaluation. MeshAnything receives sampled evaluation shapes while generation baselines sample unconditionally. Conditioning comparisons and controlled input-noise tests add further protocols; the original split, extraction metrics and training durations remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figure 3 newly compares training and validation perplexity under shape, image and unconditional inputs, testing the claimed training advantage. Appendix A.2/Table 6 adds coordinate-and-normal noise sensitivity and reconstruction from Rodin-generated inputs. The original decoder ablations remain intact as Figures 7 and Tables 3–4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v2's participant counts and preference percentages describe the new evaluation rather than an added uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds preference results, generation scores, perplexity curves and input-quality results. For example, Table 1 reports MeshAnything receiving 63.2% of shape votes and 60.7% of topology votes against generation baselines. Original decoder and Marching Cubes/remeshing values remain unchanged. The expanded extraction comparison changes the ECD leader: FlexiCubes scores 6.121 versus MeshAnything's 6.245, both scaled by 10^-2, replacing v1's best-ECD finding.

T1.justification: The conditional-distribution approximations, chain-rule argument and method equations (1)–(10) are retained. v2 adds empirical support and descriptions of evaluation metrics, but no new formal assumptions, mathematical derivations or proofs.

C1.justification: v2 adds an explicit fourth contribution claiming superiority over previous mesh-generation methods. Section 3 shifts from achieving the same targets with less training to better performance and broader applications. The central setting, architecture, integration and efficiency claims in the abstract and conclusion remain.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets smaller input-noise levels as tolerable, larger noise as substantially harmful, and Rodin results as evidence of compatibility with generated inputs. Section 5.4 attributes the new comparative advantages to shape conditioning. The existing face-count and generative-instability limitations are retained in Appendix A.3.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies a batch size of eight per GPU, identifies Rodin as the upstream generator, and explicitly describes Blender's voxel mode, noise injection and normal renormalization. These improve documentation without establishing changes to the retained training setup. Core hardware, training durations, vocabulary parameters and the project link remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Shape As Points and Rodin and removes the Dual Marching Cubes discussion and citation. It more explicitly positions evaluation against both mesh-generation and mesh-extraction methods, while retaining its principal relationship to MeshGPT. The switch to author-year citations is a presentation change.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized around generation comparisons and user studies. Original metric descriptions, detailed qualitative analysis, extraction comparisons, decoder ablations, limitations and social impact move into Appendix A. Related-work passages are condensed and the acknowledgments are removed.

P2.justification: v2 adds the two-panel perplexity figure and three tables, redraws the pipeline to distinguish training from inference, and expands the extraction-comparison table. Retained qualitative and decoder-ablation figures are collected in the appendix, substantially changing their placement and the document layout.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important gap in v1's validation by adding direct human judgments of topology quality, relevant generation and extraction comparators, and input-quality robustness tests. It preserves the original evidence and limitations and removes the obsolete best-ECD claim. Different conditioning limits the generation-superiority conclusions, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but the broader, relevant validation substantially strengthens the paper overall.
